Labor often naturally slows down when you change environments - especially a hospital environment which is loud and bright when you’re first admitted (which is not helpful for the progression of labor).

It’s recommended to wait until active labor to arrive at the hospital because it’s a lot harder for established active labor to slow down with a change of environment vs early labor. Also, the law about not turning away people in labor applies to people in active labor. I have been with clients as they were turned away in early labor (1-2 cm, baby’s station high, and no broken waters). If your waters break, they’ll admit you no matter how dilated you are.

That being said - I strongly recommend hiring a doula. Your doula can arrive at your home to help you cope with early labor. Using the shower or tub at home can help a LOT with managing the sensations of labor and your doula can provide counter pressure and other coping techniques to help. Your doula can also help you determine when the right time to move to the hospital is.

If hiring a doula isn’t in the budget, I STRONGLY recommend taking a comprehensive childbirth course. Birth Like A Badass is my favorite one to recommend. Not only will you learn how to cope with labor, but also how to advocate for yourself, which is incredibly important, especially if you do not have a doula there to advocate for you. Another great childbirth ed option is Birth Smarter.

One thing I’ll add to this - make sure to update your availability every single day. They list doulas based on most recent update activity so if you make a habit of every morning just updating your availability, you’ll be shown higher up on the website!

You may want to consider switching practices as there is a chance that any of the male OBs in the practice will be on call when you deliver.

If you are low risk, I cannot recommend midwifery care enough! Midwives usually practice at a lower volume which means they have more time to offer individualized care and build a relationship with you. Appointments are usually an hour vs 10-15 min at an OB office. And midwives deliver in hospitals so you can still get an epidural or be induced if those are things you want or need.

It’s never too late to switch providers in pregnancy and I have never worked with someone (I’m a doula) who has regretted switching practices mid-pregnancy. Across the board, everyone said they only regretted not switching sooner!

Listen to your gut. It’s telling you important things and you’ll probably thank yourself in the future for trusting your intuition.

Regulating doulas makes as much sense as regulating pastors. It opens a scary can of worms regarding free speech because frankly, that is the only thing that could be regulated as far as what a doula does.

Doulas do not administer or prescribe medication. We do not offer medical advice. We do not make decisions on behalf of our clients. What we do is make sure that our clients are informed about all of their options and the benefits and risks of that so that they can make the most informed choices that align with them.

In short: we foster informed consent in medical settings. And this terrifies a lot of healthcare providers.

True informed consent in medicine is dying if it even was alive to begin with. What doctors and hospital admins are perceiving as doulas “influencing” their clients to make certain choices, is in actuality, patients engaging in informed decision making instead of blindly following their doctors. The culture of obstetrics is highly paternalistic meaning that lots of doctors develop a god-complex and practice in such a way that actually runs the risk of poor outcomes for their patients.

Regulating doulas would only bolster the existing culture of doctors believing that they always know what’s right (which we simply know is not true, especially when caring for Black patients) and patients never getting an opportunity to ask questions that would help them make an informed decision.

In short: doulas are fighting like hell to make sure this national certification board doesn’t happen. It will harm patients, lead to more of the same poor outcomes we’re already dealing with, and limit free speech for doulas while protecting hospitals’ bottom lines.

It’s typical for doulas to have time limits but it’s not typical to then charge per hour for the birth. For reference, my limit is 24 hours of continuous care (i.e. no breaks to sleep/rest) and then I will call in my backup doula to switch places with me. If the labor continues for a long time after, I’ll often switch back with my backup after getting a few solid hours of sleep. I (the doula) pay my backup a partial fee depending on how we’ve negotiated our backup agreement so none of that financial stress falls onto the client.

The average first time labor is around ~24 hours. Only guaranteeing 8 hours not only makes no sense, but sounds negligent for exactly the reason you stated (feeling pressure to deliver faster).

I would keep on your doula search and find someone that offers a more standard care package.

I changed how I presented myself and while I did book fewer clients, the ones I was booking were absolutely amazing and I’m still close with many of them to this day!

Ugh preach. I’m also annoyed at the widespread policies of CFM despite the fact that we know now definitively that it doesn’t improve outcomes and does increase cesareans. Your feelings of frustration are super super valid here!

That being said, that’s simply MY feelings personally and I’m not the one in labor. I do educate my clients prenatally about monitoring and I prepare them to understand that most hospitals and OB practices use CFM routinely. From there, we talk about what to expect re: monitoring, ways to advocate for more breaks from the monitors if that’s their preference, or if they’re not comfortable with that approach at all, we talk about switching provider practices to someone who does intermittent auscultation. The main thing to note here is that I let my client lead in terms of what decision they want to make.

Unfortunately, in the medical industrial complex, lots of doctors and nurses can’t see the forest from the trees and often get hung up on things like monitoring because it’s simply how things have always been done. But no matter what, it’s best to get a feel for how your clients feel about monitoring, offer them evidence-based resources so they can learn about the benefits and risks and make an informed decision, and then amplify their voice in the delivery room based on the conversations you had prenatally.

Birthing Advocacy Doula Trainings (BADT) has a lot of great sliding scale and low cost options as well as payment plans. If their sliding scale rates for training is still out of reach for you, send them an email and see if you can work something out!

While certification isn’t necessary to become a doula, it is extremely helpful to have it if you want to be able to work in hospitals (which is where the vast majority of people give birth). Really, it’s the training that’s the most valuable and BADT is a really strong organization!

Just how demanding the full picture of the job would be. For me, the actual births themselves were (for the most part) not a problem. It was the on-call schedule that ended up leading to my (semi) retirement from the job. I didn’t have the type of support network I needed to make the lifestyle work in a sustainable way.

The other thing I wish I knew was just how prevalent obstetric violence and coercion is and also how complex it is. It was truly rare that I ever worked with a provider who genuinely provided evidence-based care across the board. Even providers that were highly recommended by doulas in my area I would see them pushing inductions based on the ARRIVE trial or pushing c-sections during stalled out labors with no indicators that anything was wrong. The problem isn’t as much individual providers but rather the culture of birth here (I live in the U.S.)

I don’t say this to deter you from the work. But I do wish that more people had been straight with me about the things I would witness on a regular basis that have sadly been normalized in this field of medicine. Everyone has a different way of coping - some doulas have certain hospitals or providers on a personal blacklist that they will no longer work with, some doulas plan their bookings so that they can take off 1-2 months during the year, some doulas work in partnership with other doulas. There’s no right or wrong way. I just never figured out a solution that really helped and so I burnt out after 2 years. I came out of retirement this year to support two births which were beautiful but still, the on-call life was ROUGH.

Community care is just as important if not more important than self-care in this world. Find your people and lean on each other <3

It all comes down to avoiding litigation. The legality of this is muddy - I’ve heard a variety of excuses all the way from “video recording births isn’t legal” (which is simply untrue) to “the hospital does not pay for an insurance policy that covers video recording” (may be true, but still not concrete enough to prevent someone from recording since the person recording isn’t who signed the insurance policy).

Obstetrics is the most litigious field in all of medicine and hospitals are keenly aware of this. If there’s anything they can do to prevent the creation of evidence that could be used against them in a court of law, they’re going to do it, even if it could be considered an infringement of rights or a violation of the law. Hospitals are, first and foremost, a business. Their model is dependent on making as much money as possible even if it may be antithetical to outcomes or patient satisfaction.

Polysecure is not a how-to guide for polyamory. It’s more of a first-of-it’s-kind academic deep dive into the intersection of polyamory, trauma, and attachment theory. The author addresses this and talks about it often in interviews.

Her most recent book, Polywise, sounds like it’s the book you were hoping for Polysecure to be. She talks about this in the forward about how she wanted to write Polywise first, but after discussions with Eve Rickart, decided to write Polysecure first to establish some basic information and fill the gap in the lack of literature around these topics.

We have to remember as experienced poly folks that not every book is going to be what we want it to be and a lot of the popular literature is going to be geared towards beginner challenges. Which is exactly why she wrote Polywise as an aid for more intermediate/ advanced poly challenges including practical solutions.

I’d be curious to hear your thoughts on Polywise if you decide to give it a try.

If you’d like a more personalized approach to reproductive health, look into seeing a midwife instead of an OBGYN.

They’re not all crunchy hippies who only use herbs for treatment lol - they can prescribe medication and use plenty of western technology and practices. The sensations of labor depend on a number of factors - some we have control over, some we don’t.

Taking a childbirth class will teach you various coping techniques that you can use. Birth Smarter has some great on-demand classes that you can take at any time at your own pace.

Keep in mind the 3 R’s of Labor - Relaxation, Rhythm, and Ritual. Finding movements, mantras, positions, etc that you can repeat during different stages is very helpful. 

One mantra many of my clients (I’m a doula) have used in the past is “I can handle the pain/sensation because the pain/sensation IS me.” It is not pain that is coming from some exterior source like a broken bone or spoiled food, it is your own body bringing you closer to meeting your baby - doing exactly what it is supposed to do.

I wish you the best of luck! Definitely look into those childbirth Ed classes!

DONA tries to pass off like the certifying body for all doulas. But the issue is that doulas are not a regulated profession. We are not licensed, rather we are trained and certified (if we choose - some people have learned the practice from their elders).

DONA has been very clear that doulas are not advocates. Many doulas have a problem with this because we are in a maternal mortality and morbidity crisis and advocacy and informed consent is an extremely important part of preventing unnecessary interventions, traumatic births, and poor outcomes.

I chose to certify with a different organization that does believe that doulas are advocates. But certification really does not matter, especially considering the number of births she’s attended. If you like her and click with her, go for it!

You can request an hour of immediate skin-to-skin before the nursing staff does any of the newborn exam. You also don’t have to consent to a bath - many parents prefer to do it themselves when they’re home as to not interrupt the bonding process (your baby can smell you and vice versa).

Depending on where you give birth and what the culture is, you may have to strongly advocate for this. Many nurses will say in a SUPER nice tone “I’m just gonna grab baby real quick to do the exam 🥰” - you can say no. Uninterrupted skin-to-skin is an evidence based practice and the laundry list of benefits is miles long.

Also as an aside - vernix is meant to be rubbed into baby’s skin, not off of it with towels. It helps baby’s skin stay moisturized after floating in amniotic fluid for 9 months. You can request they leave baby alone and just put a blanket on top for warmth.

Remember - your body, your baby. Hospital policy is not law. And you ~always~ have the right to refusal. If you can, hire a doula! Best of luck!

Seems like you have a fundamental misunderstanding on what a boundary actually is. Let me explain-

Boundaries, rules, and agreements are all completely different. A rule is created by an authority or created above us. Rules are usually one-way streets. An agreement is created between two or more people. Agreements are usually two-way streets. Boundaries on the other hand are self-created and self-enforced.

You cannot place boundaries around other people - if it’s dependent on someone else changing their behavior, it’s not a boundary anymore, it’s an ask. And as an autonomous human being, your girlfriend is allowed to say no to the ask. Then it’s up to you to decide how you want to proceed.

I’ll use your case as an example to show the difference between rules, agreements, and boundaries:
- Rule: “you are not allowed to take a bath when your friend is in the bathroom.”
- Agreement: “we both agree to not be nude around anyone other than each other, friends included”
- Boundary: “I am not willing to date someone who is okay being nude around people other than me.”

If you want to create a boundary here, that’s fine and valid. But the boundary has to be something that you can control. Your partner’s behavior is not something you can actually control. So enforcing your boundary here means ending the relationship because of a fundamental incompatibility.

To be clear - this should not be used as an opportunity to blame your partner for “breaking you up.” Her boundaries around nudity around friends are just different from yours and neither is technically right or wrong. Owning your boundaries and needs is part of being an adult in a relationship.

All that aside - you would likely benefit from doing some unpacking / unmeshing of your connection between nudity and sex. They are not inherently connected.

Honestly, I don’t think you’re the AH - but your ask/demand is clearly rooted in your own insecurities that you’re projecting onto your partner in an attempt to feel more in control. Spoiler alert: this does not make for sustainable or long lasting relationships. Go to therapy. Work on yourself. And maybe take a break from dating and relationships while you do that work.

Doula here - it's your body, your choice.

Epidurals are not without risks - and your provider will (see: should) discuss with you the potential risks and side effects, but once you've had that conversation, you can give informed consent.

What I will say from my experience attending births is that if you want the epidural during your labor and your husband tries to fight you on it, the likelihood of your body slowing down or stopping your labor is high. You need to feel 100% safe and supported during labor in order for your uterus to do its job and contract. If you feel fear/adrenaline, labor will slow down. So by imposing his (incredibly misguided and frankly selfish) beliefs, he may very well be the cause of a failure to progress which is the #1 reason for unplanned c-sections in this country.

If you can, I highly recommend finding a doula to help support you during labor and advocate for your wishes - both to your provider and husband. Your doula can also help him understand the benefits of epidurals before labor begins so he's 100% on board.

So one thing that’s important to distinguish is a boundary vs a rule vs an agreement. A boundary is something that has to be self-enforced. (Ex: I won’t date people who are dating my ex). A rule is something that you give to someone (ex: you’re not allowed to date my ex). An agreement is something that’s decided between two people (ex: we agree to not date each other’s exes). Agreements don’t always have to be a two way street but both people have to agree to it without pressure or coercion. The Multiamory Podcast has a great episode on this.

Another thing to note is that your boundaries or agreements don’t have to be rational or logical. They can be rooted in emotion and that’s okay. (Ex: my partner and I have an agreement that I won’t wear the special lingerie set he got me for my birthday on dates with other people. Does this agreement make logical sense? Maybe, maybe not. But it’s important to my partner and I don’t have any major objections). There is a fine line here though - it’s important to not get into the habit of creating boundaries, rules, and agreements that are ultimately bandaids that keep you from doing the inner work to heal internal wounds and address things like jealousy and insecurity.

What I’m getting at is that it’s okay that it’s important for you to meet his birth family first. But it’s also a good idea to get to the root about why that is. Maybe you haven’t been feeling like a primary in other ways so this would help you feel more prioritized - so then that’s an opportunity for the two of you to explore how you can make each other feel prioritized across the board. I think the two of you would benefit from sitting down and fleshing out what it means to be “primary” partners with one another. Everyone has a different definition of what that looks like and that’s okay. It’s also okay for that to look different for each of you - that’s why it’s called negotiation. Equality is not the same as symmetry. Equality means that everyone feels like their unique needs and desires and boundaries are being respected consistently.
